{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-chebyshev}
#### Chebyshev's inequality

Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mean$ and finite variance $\varpar > 0$.
Then for every $k > 0$:

$$
\Prf{\abs{X - \mean} \ge k\sdpar} \le \frac{1}{k^2}
$$

:::

::: proof

The random variable $(X - \mean)^2$ is nonnegative,
and its expectation is $\varpar$.
Because $\abs{X - \mean} \ge k\sdpar$ exactly when $(X - \mean)^2 \ge k^2\varpar$,
@thm-markov gives

$$
\Prf{\abs{X - \mean} \ge k\sdpar}
= \Prf{(X - \mean)^2 \ge k^2\varpar}
\le \frac{\varpar}{k^2\varpar}
= \frac{1}{k^2}
$$

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

@thm-chebyshev needs only a mean and a variance, not a distribution,
so it holds for every distribution that has them.
That generality makes it loose:
for a normal distribution, the chance of landing more than two standard deviations from the mean is about 5%, but the bound at $k = 2$ is 25%.

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

Bienaymé derived this bound in 1853 [@bienayme1853],
and Chebyshev proved a more general form in 1867 [@tchebichef1867].
A modern treatment is in [@blitzstein2019introduction].

:::
